result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.max_weight_matching()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find a maximum weight matching in the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L21984-L22074){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.max_weight_matching() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Finds a matching that maximizes the sum of edge weights. Uses a greedy algorithm that selects edges by weight in descending order. For unweighted graphs, all edges have weight `1.0`. Note that this is a greedy approximation, not guaranteed to be optimal for general graphs. For optimal solutions on bipartite graphs, use specialized bipartite matching algorithms. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of edge IDs forming a maximum weight matching. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} - time complexity: `O(E log E)` for sorting edges - space complexity: `O(V + E)` for tracking matched nodes and edges - greedy approximation: selects heaviest edges first - not guaranteed to be optimal for general graphs - optimal for trees and forests - for bipartite graphs, consider Hungarian algorithm - for unweighted graphs, equivalent to maximal matching ## Examples {.doc-examples} Given a choice between one heavy edge (`A-B`, weight 10) and several light ones, the greedy algorithm grabs the heavy edge first, then fills in the rest of the matching with whatever's left: ::: {#c3cec7df .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(weighted=True) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_node(label="D") .add_edge("A", "B", weight=10.0) .add_edge("B", "C", weight=1.0) .add_edge("C", "D", weight=1.0) .add_edge("A", "C", weight=2.0) ) matching = graph.max_weight_matching() # Returns total weight of the matching (11.0: edges A-B and C-D) sum(graph.get_edge(eid).weight for eid in matching) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 11.0 ``` ::: ::: For an unweighted graph, every edge has the same implicit weight, so the algorithm just maximizes the number of matched pairs -- here, a complete graph on 8 nodes yields a perfect matching: ::: {#9d413051 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_full_graph(8) matching = graph.max_weight_matching() # Returns 4 (all 8 nodes paired up) len(matching) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 4 ``` ::: ::: Being greedy, this can miss the true optimum: in a triangle with a heavy `A-B` edge, the algorithm locks in `A-B` first, leaving `C` unmatched, even though a different weighting could favor a different pair: ::: {#88881d53 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(weighted=True) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_edge("A", "B", weight=5.0) .add_edge("B", "C", weight=3.0) .add_edge("A", "C", weight=2.0) ) matching = graph.max_weight_matching() # Returns 1 (only one edge can be chosen in a 3-node graph) len(matching) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 1 ``` ::: :::
